brief.topic: The Quiet Curve Inside a Cooling Cup

s01: A warm cup of tea changes fastest when it is furthest from the room around it.
As that temperature gap closes, the cooling slows.
Imagine a room at twenty degrees, and tea at eighty.
In this simple model, each equal stretch of time cuts the remaining gap in half.
Sixty becomes thirty, then fifteen, then seven and a half.
It is the distance above room temperature, not the temperature itself.
The tea goes from eighty to fifty, then thirty-five.
Twenty degrees stays underneath every step.
Connect those moments and a curve appears.
A large gap gives a steep fall.
A small gap gives a gentle approach.
This is exponential cooling toward a surrounding temperature.
The halving time depends on the cup and its surroundings.
Real tea also evaporates, and air can move.
This model assumes a steady room and a constant cooling factor.
Even a cooling cup can invite us to notice how change responds to difference.

scenes.narration:
A warm cup of tea changes fastest when it is furthest from the room around it. As that temperature gap closes, the cooling slows.

Imagine a room at twenty degrees, and tea at eighty. The gap is sixty degrees. In this simple model, each equal stretch of time cuts the remaining gap in half. Sixty becomes thirty, then fifteen, then seven and a half.

Notice what is being halved. It is the distance above room temperature, not the temperature itself. The tea goes from eighty to fifty, then thirty-five. Twenty degrees stays underneath every step.

Connect those moments and a curve appears. A large gap gives a steep fall. A small gap gives a gentle approach. This is exponential cooling toward a surrounding temperature.

The halving time depends on the cup and its surroundings. Real tea also evaporates, and air can move. This model assumes a steady room and a constant cooling factor. Even a cooling cup can invite us to notice how change responds to difference.
